nameStory: The northeastern bulrush gets its name from its limited range in the northeastern United States, where it's become incredibly rare. It's also called barbedbristle bulrush because of the distinctive hooked, tooth-like spines that develop on its fruits - like tiny barbed wire that helps you identify this endangered plant.
description: Northeastern bulrush is an extremely rare sedge that forms clumps of slender, upright or leaning stems in wetlands. This endangered plant grows from fibrous underground stems called rhizomes and reaches up to about 2 feet tall. Its narrow, grass-like leaves can be over 2 feet long but only about half an inch wide, and it produces small clusters of brown, oval-shaped flower spikes at the stem tips.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The developing fruits have straight or curved toothed spines that feel rough to the touch - this barbed bristle feature is the most reliable way to identify this rare plant

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small oval clusters of brown scales with green midribs, each cluster less than half an inch long, appearing at stem tips and sometimes along the upper stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, grass-like leaves up to 2 feet long but only about half an inch wide, with a smooth texture typical of sedges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps of upright or leaning stems from underground rhizomes, sometimes producing small bulb-like growths along the stems

habitat: This extremely rare plant grows in variable-depth wetlands including beaver ponds, sandy depressions, and especially sinkhole ponds in sandstone bedrock that fill with spring water and dry out in summer. In New England, it's found in scattered locations from New Hampshire south, often in areas with fluctuating water levels. With only 3 recorded observations in all of New England, you're more likely to win the lottery than stumble across this federally endangered species.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate around March, with new shoots emerging from rhizomes in May as water levels are typically at their highest in seasonal wetlands.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in June and July with small brown flower clusters, followed by the distinctive barbed fruits developing from July through September.
seasonality.fall: Fruits mature and disperse in early fall, while the above-ground portions begin to die back as seasonal ponds may be drying out.
seasonality.winter: Plants are dormant with only the underground rhizome system surviving, making identification impossible during this season.

funFact: This plant is so rare that it was thought to be completely extinct in New York state until a single population was rediscovered in 2010 - imagine the excitement of that botanist who found a species that was presumed gone forever!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other bulrushes in wetlands, but the distinctive barbed spines on the fruits are unique - if you can gently feel tiny hooks or teeth on the developing seeds, you may have found this botanical treasure.
contextualKnowledge: This is a federally endangered species, so if you think you've found it, don't disturb it but do report your sighting to local botanists or conservation authorities - your observation could be scientifically important for tracking this rare plant's survival.
compareHints: Unlike its close relative mosquito bulrush which it sometimes hybridizes with, northeastern bulrush has those distinctive barbed bristles on its fruits. Most other bulrushes in the genus like woolgrass or dark green bulrush grow in more permanent wetlands and lack these hooked spines. The combination of seasonal wetland habitat and barbed fruits makes this species unique among New England's bulrushes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woolgrass can be distinguished from other bulrushes in its genus by its particularly fluffy, wool-like seed heads with prominent bristles.

Among its bulrush relatives, panicled bulrush stands out with its distinctly loose, branching flower cluster - woolgrass has a denser, more cotton-like appearance, while nodding bulrush has drooping clusters on curved branches.
**Uncertain comparisons** - Unlike the robust woolgrass or dark green bulrush which form substantial clumps, mosquito bulrush likely maintains a more delicate, scattered growth pattern.
Among New England's bulrushes, dark green bulrush stands out for its robust size and deep green color.

Among its Scirpus relatives, black-girdle bulrush is the only one with the distinctive dark stem bands - woolgrass has woolly flower heads, dark green bulrush lacks the bands and is more robust, and panicled bulrush has much larger, more open flower clusters.
Among its Scirpus relatives in New England, nodding bulrush stands out for its distinctly drooping flower clusters - most other bulrushes like woolgrass have more upright, dense flower heads.
Among its bulrush relatives, Long's bulrush stands out for its coastal habitat preference and rare flowering habit - most other bulrushes in the genus flower more regularly.

**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Unlike its wetland relatives like woolgrass and dark green bulrush which form dense stands in sunny marshes, Woodland Beakrush grows in small, scattered clumps in shaded forests.
Among its bulrush relatives in New England, Georgia bulrush is much less common than woolgrass or dark green bulrush, which you're more likely to encounter in similar wet habitats.

Among New England bulrushes, leafy bulrush stands out for having numerous well-developed leaves along the stem, while woolgrass has a more densely clustered, wool-like flower head, and dark green bulrush tends to be shorter with darker foliage.
Among New England's bulrushes, stalked bulrush is the only one with flower clusters that hang from individual stalks rather than sitting directly on the main stem.
